clue.text: VAT, say, for nails

indicators.note: say tells us to take the word as spoken, matching a word with a different spelling

parts.note: VAT, value added tax, is a tax

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a sales tax could be swapped for some ironmongery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'VAT, say' looks like 'for example VAT', but VAT is an example of a TAX, and 'say' then gives a word that sounds like TAX: TACKS.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacks are small broad-headed nails used for fixing carpet or fabric.

clue.text: They make their names as proverbial listeners

definitions.text: They make their names as proverbial listeners

parts.words: They make their names as proverbial listeners
parts.note: refers to the saying 'tell it to' a certain corps of sea soldiers, said to believe any tall story

explanation.surface: People who become famous for being good at hearing others out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell that to the marines' is an old saying meaning 'I don't believe you', once implying sea soldiers would swallow any tale.
explanation.definitionFit: The British corps of seagoing soldiers features in the saying used to dismiss an implausible story.

clue.text: Two birds seen in early part of the day

parts.note: a cock is a male bird, especially a rooster
a crow is a large black bird

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher spots two species just after dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two birds' gives COCK and CROW in turn; 'seen in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockcrow is dawn, the time when roosters first call.

clue.text: Picadors are involved here and there

indicators.note: being involved suggests being tangled up, so the letters of Picadors are rearranged

explanation.surface: Bullfighters on horseback take part in the corrida at scattered points.
explanation.walkthrough: Picadors are mounted bullfighters; 'are involved' signals the anagram of PICADORS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporadic means occurring at scattered, irregular places or times.

clue.text: You're out of spirits when he leaves

definitions.text: You're out of spirits when he leaves

parts.words: You're out of spirits when he leaves
parts.note: reads like a barman leaving a dry house, but describes a priest whose departure means the demons have been driven out

explanation.surface: Once a certain visitor goes, the drinks cabinet is bare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' suggests drink; here it means ghosts or demons, and being 'out of' them means they have been cast out.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest who performs rites of expulsion drives evil beings from a person or place, leaving it free of them.

clue.text: Repeat after some reflection

parts.note: sounds like repeating something after thinking it over, but describes a sound bounced back off a surface

explanation.surface: Advice to say something again only once you have thought about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reflection' suggests careful thought; here it is sound waves bouncing back.
explanation.definitionFit: An echo is sound heard again when it bounces off a wall or cliff.

clue.text: Stay to check mother in

indicators.note: in places the word for mother inside the word for check

parts.note: to rein is to check or restrain, as with a horse
ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: A request to stay and keep an eye on mother at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' is a link; 'check' is REIN (restrain), not 'inspect'.
explanation.definitionFit: To remain is to stay where one is.

clue.text: Encourage a sound location for a pub

indicators.note: sound tells us these words are to be heard, matching a word spelt differently

parts.note: a pub is an inn, and a location is a site

explanation.surface: Someone urges choosing a solid spot to open a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A sound location' looks like 'a good location'; 'sound' is the homophone signal for INN SITE.
explanation.definitionFit: To incite is to urge on or stir up someone to act.

clue.text: Yet it may be sweet

parts.note: plays on a word meaning sour that is also a pastry, which can have a sugary filling

explanation.surface: A remark that something might still turn out pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: As an adjective the word means sharp or sour, hence 'yet'; as a noun it is a pastry dish, often sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A tart is a pastry case with a filling such as jam or fruit, though the adjective means sharp-tasting.

clue.text: Intrude by chance or mistake

indicators.note: a mistake garbles things, so the letters of chance and or are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone trespasses, either accidentally or through an error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' is a link; 'mistake' signals the anagram of CHANCE OR.
explanation.definitionFit: To encroach is to advance gradually beyond proper limits onto another's territory, an intrusion.

clue.text: Player given an awful roasting

indicators.note: awful suggests something badly done, so the letters of roasting are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A sportsman gets a terrible dressing-down from critics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests a sportsman, but here it is a musician; 'awful' signals the anagram of ROASTING.
explanation.definitionFit: A church musician who plays the pipe organ performs on an instrument, so is a player.

clue.text: Investigation reaches wrong outcome after right start

indicators.note: after places the scrambled letters following that opening letter
start means the opening letter of the word right is taken
a wrong outcome suggests something gone awry, so the letters of reaches are jumbled

explanation.surface: An inquiry reaches a false conclusion despite a good beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outcome' looks like part of the definition's story, but 'wrong outcome' together is the anagram signal; 'start' takes only the opening letter of 'right'.
explanation.definitionFit: Research is systematic study to establish facts, a form of inquiry.

clue.text: I hit out after a double century and get applause

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: double means the letter for century is written twice

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a century in cricket

indicators.note: out here signals that the word for hit lies outside, enclosing the I

parts.note: lam is an informal word meaning hit or thrash
taken as written

explanation.surface: A batsman reaches two hundred, lashes out, and the crowd applauds.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture of a batsman reaching two hundred and lashing out disguises a plain charade; 'hit' is the informal verb lam, and 'out' sets it outside the I.
explanation.definitionFit: Acclaim is enthusiastic public praise, the kind shown by clapping.

clue.text: Mother's pets are dogs

parts.note: ma is mother, with the possessive s
a pet is a fit of sulking, and a tiff is a petty quarrel

explanation.surface: Mum's beloved animals are canines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pets' looks like animals but means sulks or quarrels, TIFFS; 'are' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Mastiffs are a breed of large, powerful guard dog.

clue.text: The more there are, the fewer there are

definitions.text: The more there are, the fewer there are

parts.words: The more there are, the fewer there are
parts.note: a paradox resolved by thinking of people missing from a gathering: more of them means fewer present

explanation.surface: A riddle about numbers that both grow and shrink at once.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'there are' means 'are there, present': each extra missing person lowers the count of those in attendance.
explanation.definitionFit: People who stay away from school or work are those not present, so each one reduces attendance.

clue.text: Used by riders but not as riding breeches

definitions.text: Used by riders but not as riding breeches

parts.words: Used by riders but not as riding breeches
parts.note: bags is old slang for trousers, but these are pouches hung from a horse's seat

explanation.surface: Something horse riders use, though not as their jodhpurs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags' is old British slang for loose trousers, so riding 'bags' could be breeches; the clue rules that out.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddlebags are pouches slung across a horse behind the seat to carry belongings.

clue.text: The Met office

parts.note: looks like the British weather service, but Met is the Metropolitan Police and the office is its headquarters

explanation.surface: A reference to Britain's national weather forecasting service.
explanation.walkthrough: The Met Office is the UK weather service; the Met is also London's Metropolitan Police, whose headquarters carries this famous name.
explanation.definitionFit: This London building has been the headquarters of the Metropolitan Police Service since the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Riding school discipline is a habit that comes with time

parts.note: a habit is a dress, as in a riding habit or a nun's habit
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Horsemanship training as a practice that develops over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' suggests routine; here it is clothing, a DRESS, with AGE added.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressage is the training of a horse in precise movements, a competitive equestrian discipline.

clue.text: They fly to Riva as a change

indicators.note: a change means altering the order of the letters of to Riva as

explanation.surface: Travellers take a plane to Riva on Lake Garda for a different holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Riva is an Italian lakeside resort; 'as a change' looks like 'for variety', but 'a change' signals the anagram of TO RIVA AS.
explanation.definitionFit: Aviators are pilots, people who fly aircraft.

clue.text: New proof is put to ninety-nine, half asleep

indicators.note: put to means placed next to, so the following piece is attached after the first
new suggests something made afresh, so the letters of proof is are reshaped into a fresh order

parts.note: IC is ninety-nine in Roman numerals, one less than C

explanation.surface: A tired person checks a fresh printer's proof at ninety-nine percent drowsiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half asleep' is the definition, soporific meaning drowsy; 'put to' joins the pieces. Ninety-nine as IC is an informal Roman form, one before C.
explanation.definitionFit: Soporific can describe someone drowsy and sleepy, as well as something that induces slumber.

clue.text: Pet journal distributed around the first of May

indicators.note: distributed around means the word for journal is spread around the next letter

parts.note: a journal is a newspaper, a paper

indicators.note: the first of means taking the opening letter of May

explanation.surface: A newspaper about pets is handed out at the start of May.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' is the verb, to fondle or spoil.
explanation.definitionFit: To pamper someone is to indulge and spoil them, as one pets a favourite.

clue.text: Private line to the Queen?

parts.note: a rank is a line, as of soldiers or taxis
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen

explanation.surface: A personal telephone line to the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like an adjective, but it is a soldier of the lowest rank; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A ranker is a soldier in the ranks, such as a private, rather than an officer.

clue.text: Captive may be shot a long time afterwards

indicators.note: afterwards places the long period after the rearranged letters
may be hints the letters of shot could be in another arrangement

parts.note: an age is a long time

explanation.surface: A prisoner might be executed many years later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' looks like the captive's fate, but 'may be' makes it anagram fodder; 'afterwards' sets the long time after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hostage is a person held prisoner to secure demands, a captive.

clue.text: Monotony of a Massenet composition

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so the letters of Massenet are arranged into a new word

explanation.surface: A complaint that a piece by the French opera composer Massenet is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: Massenet was a French composer, which makes 'composition' look like his music; it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Tameness is a lack of excitement or spirit, a dull sameness.

clue.text: Secured the same numbers of points?

definitions.meaning: fastened, as with a rope or knot
level on score, drawing a game

explanation.definitionFit: Tied means fastened with a knot, and also level in a contest, both sides having scored equally.

clue.text: Chinese capital lies in total waste

indicators.note: lies in places the capital letter inside the word for total

parts.note: a sum is a total

indicators.note: capital means the first letter, here of Chinese

explanation.surface: Beijing is buried in rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chinese capital' wants to be Beijing; it is the capital letter C.
explanation.definitionFit: Scum is refuse or worthless matter, as on a dirty surface.

clue.text: Italian man of affairs

parts.note: suggests a businessman from Italy, but the affairs are romantic ones, pointing to a famous Venetian seducer

explanation.surface: A description of a businessman from Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affairs' suggests business; here it means love affairs. Giacomo Casanova was an eighteenth-century Venetian adventurer famed for his seductions.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venetian adventurer's name has become a byword for a womaniser with many lovers.

clue.text: Place set aside for development

parts.note: sounds like land reserved for building, but development here is processing photographic film

explanation.surface: A plot of land earmarked for new building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Development' suggests property; in photography, film is developed in a room kept free of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Photographic film and prints are processed in an unlit room so that light does not spoil them.

clue.text: See as new comforts

indicators.note: new suggests something remade, so the letters of see and as are put into a fresh order

explanation.surface: An instruction to regard something with fresh eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See as new' reads like 'look at afresh'; 'new' signals the anagram of SEE AS.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease someone is to relieve their pain or worry, which is to comfort them.
